pos: n. (a young unmarried woman; a female servant; rendering Hebrew shiphchah, amah, Greek pais)
etymology: Saxon mægden, a young woman. In Scripture the maid is usually the least person in the household — which is exactly why God keeps putting her at the centre of the story.
biblical_def: A maid in Scripture is a young woman, commonly a servant, and commonly the least considered person in the house. Scripture keeps giving her the decisive line. A captive girl carried off in a raid tells her mistress where healing is to be found: “the Syrians had gone out by companies, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maid; and she waited on Naaman's wife” (2Ki 5:2) — and the general of Syria is cleansed because a slave girl spoke. Hagar the Egyptian handmaid becomes the occasion of Abram's worst failure of faith: “she had an handmaid, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar” (Gen 16:1), and the God who sees hears her in the wilderness. The psalmist makes the maid's posture the model of the believer's prayer: “as the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress; so our eyes wait upon the LORD our God, until that he have mercy upon us” (Psa 123:2) — watching the hand, not the clock. And to a dead twelve-year-old our Lord speaks the tenderest imperative in the Gospels: “Maid, arise” (Luk 8:54).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines maid as an unmarried woman, a virgin, and also a woman servant — both senses present throughout the Authorized Version.
webster_full: MAID, n. An unmarried woman, or a young unmarried woman; a virgin.
2. A female servant.
3. A man who has had no commerce with women; a sense now rare.
MAIDEN, n. A maid; a virgin; a young woman unmarried.
scriptures: And the Syrians had gone out by companies, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maid; and she waited on Naaman's wife.
Gen 16:1
Now Sarai Abram's wife bare him no children: and she had an handmaid, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar.

Behold, as the eyes of servants look unto the hand of their masters, and as the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress; so our eyes wait upon the LORD our God, until that he have mercy upon us.
Luk 8:54
And he put them all out, and took her by the hand, and called, saying, Maid, arise.
corruption_summary: Service has been recast as an indignity to be escaped rather than a station in which God is glorified, so the maid of Scripture is read as a victim of her circumstances instead of an instrument of God within them.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern reflex on reading of a servant girl is to ask how she can be liberated from the role, and the question is not wrong — Scripture has a great deal to say about how servants must be treated, and Nehemiah rebuked nobles who exacted usury of their brethren. But the reflex becomes a corruption when it makes the station itself the whole story, so that nothing a servant does within it can count. The little maid of 2 Kings 5 is not waiting for a change of circumstances to be useful to God. She is a captive in an enemy house, and from there she redirects a Syrian general to the prophet of Israel.

Psalm 123 shows why Scripture treats the position with such honour. The maid watching her mistress's hand is the picture of faith itself: attentive, unhurried, dependent, expecting the smallest signal to be enough. Our Lord took the form of a servant, and told His disciples that the greatest among them should be servant of all. A culture that can only see servanthood as demotion has lost the ability to read either the maid or the Master.
roots_summary: Hebrew shiphchah (H8198) and amah (H519), maidservant, handmaid; Greek pais (G3816), a child or servant — the least in the house, and often the hinge of the narrative.
roots_lines: Hebrew shiphchah (H8198) — maidservant, handmaid; Hagar in Abram's house (Gen 16:1).
Hebrew amah (H519) — handmaid, female slave; the word Mary echoes in her handmaid of the Lord (Luk 1:38, Greek doulē).
Greek pais (G3816) — a child, boy or girl, also a servant; “Maid, arise” (Luk 8:54).
usage: “A little maid; and she waited on Naaman's wife” — the captive who knew where healing was.
“As the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress” — the posture of waiting faith.
“Maid, arise” — two words spoken over a dead child.

pos: n. (a boy, a youth, a young male servant; rendering Hebrew na'ar, Greek paidarion)
etymology: Of northern origin, a boy or stripling. The Hebrew na'ar covers everything from a small child to a young attendant, and Scripture's great scenes keep turning on one.
biblical_def: A lad is a boy or young servant, and Scripture repeatedly makes him the point on which a whole history turns. On Moriah, Abraham leaves the servants behind: “Abide ye here with the ass; and I and the lad will go yonder and worship, and come again to you” (Gen 22:5) — the lad is Isaac, the son of promise carrying the wood for his own offering, and Abraham's come again to you is faith speaking of resurrection before there was a word for it. In the wilderness, a boy dying of thirst is heard: “God heard the voice of the lad” (Gen 21:17), and the same verse says it twice, for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is. And on a Galilean hillside a boy's packed lunch feeds a multitude: “There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?” (Joh 6:9) — Andrew's arithmetic is impeccable and entirely beside the point. A lad in Scripture is the small, uncounted thing that God takes up: the son on the altar, the boy under the shrub, the loaves in the basket.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lad as a young man or boy, a stripling — used familiarly, and in Scripture often of a young servant or attendant.
webster_full: LAD, n. A young man or boy; a stripling.
2. In familiar language, a man; a compellation of familiarity or slight contempt.
LADDIE, n. A young lad; a term of endearment.
scriptures: Gen 22:5
And Abraham said unto his young men, Abide ye here with the ass; and I and the lad will go yonder and worship, and come again to you.
And God heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her, What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is.
Joh 6:9
There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?
Luk 8:54
And he put them all out, and took her by the hand, and called, saying, Maid, arise.
corruption_summary: Boys are increasingly treated as defective men — problems of energy to be medicated or educated out — where Scripture treats a lad as a soul God hears and a servant God uses before he is grown.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors squeeze the biblical lad from opposite sides. One infantilises him indefinitely, extending boyhood well past the years in which Scripture expects a young man to be at work, bearing responsibility, and answering for himself. The other pathologises him, treating the ordinary appetites and restlessness of a boy as a disorder to be managed rather than a strength to be trained and aimed. Neither reads Genesis 22, where a lad old enough to carry the wood is old enough to be told what is happening and to submit to it.

Scripture's own approach is training with real stakes. David keeping sheep, Samuel ministering before Eli, Joseph at seventeen, the boy with the loaves — each is given something to do that actually matters, and each is answerable. And Genesis 21 guards the whole from becoming mere achievement: God heard the voice of the lad where he is. Before a boy is useful he is heard, and a father who reverses that order will raise a servant but not a son.
roots_summary: Hebrew na'ar (H5288), a boy, lad, young man, attendant; Greek paidarion (G3808), a little boy — the small figure at the centre of the great scenes.
roots_lines: Hebrew na'ar (H5288) — boy, lad, youth, servant; used of Isaac on Moriah (Gen 22:5) and of Ishmael under the shrub (Gen 21:17).
Greek paidarion (G3808) — a little boy; the lad with the five barley loaves (Joh 6:9).
The same Hebrew word describes Samuel ministering before the LORD, being a child (1Sa 2:18) — a lad in the sanctuary.
usage: “I and the lad will go yonder and worship, and come again to you” — faith speaking in the plural.
“God heard the voice of the lad where he is” — heard before he was useful.
“There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves” — the small supply God multiplies.

pos: n. pl. (men of rank and station; rendering Hebrew addir, chor, Greek eugenēs)
etymology: From Latin nobilis, well-known, of high birth. Scripture judges nobility by what a man does with his station, not by the station itself.
biblical_def: The nobles are the men of station and means, and Scripture weighs them by their conduct. Nehemiah records the most damning half-verse about a social class in the Bible: the Tekoites repaired the wall, “but their nobles put not their necks to the work of their Lord” (Neh 3:5) — the commoners built and the gentlemen would not stoop. Numbers preserves the opposite picture, nobles at labour and glad of it: “The princes digged the well, the nobles of the people digged it, by the direction of the lawgiver, with their staves” (Num 21:18). Paul notes that God's call does not run chiefly through such men: “not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called” (1Co 1:26). And Luke redefines the word altogether. Of the Bereans he writes, “These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) — nobility measured by an open Bible and an honest mind.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines noble as of exalted rank, illustrious, and also as magnanimous, of a great and generous mind — and the nobles as persons of rank above commoners.
webster_full: NOBLE, a. Great; elevated; dignified; being above every thing that can dishonor reputation.
2. Exalted; elevated; sublime.
3. Illustrious; distinguished from commoners by rank and title.
NOBLE, n. A person of rank above a commoner; a nobleman.
scriptures: Neh 3:5
And next unto them the Tekoites repaired; but their nobles put not their necks to the work of their Lord.
The princes digged the well, the nobles of the people digged it, by the direction of the lawgiver, with their staves. And from the wilderness they went to Mattanah:
For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called:
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
corruption_summary: Nobility has been reduced to a matter of birth or of brand, and separately dismissed as an oppressive category altogether — where Scripture keeps the word and redefines it by the readiness to labour and to search the scriptures.
corruption_paragraphs: One error keeps the title and drops the duty: a class that expects deference and declines the wall, which is precisely the sin Nehemiah pinned on the nobles of Tekoa. The other error abolishes the category, treating every distinction of rank as oppression to be dismantled. Scripture does neither. It records rank as a fact of the world, refuses to let rank exempt a man from work, and then quietly awards the adjective to a group of Berean synagogue-goers whose distinction was that they checked the apostle's preaching against the text.

That reassignment is the heart of the matter. Luke could have called the Bereans teachable or diligent; he called them more noble, taking the highest social word available and attaching it to daily searching of the scriptures. Paul's note in 1 Corinthians completes the picture from God's side: not many noble are called, so that no flesh should glory in His presence. The kingdom has an aristocracy, and its qualification is an open Bible.
roots_summary: Hebrew addir (H117), mighty, majestic, and chor (H2715), noble or freeman; Greek eugenēs (G2104), well-born — the word Luke gives to Bible-searchers.
roots_lines: Hebrew chor (H2715) — noble, freeman; the nobles who would not put their necks to the work (Neh 3:5).
Hebrew addir (H117) — majestic, mighty, noble; used of the nobles of the people (Num 21:18) and of the LORD Himself as glorious.
Greek eugenēs (G2104) — well-born, noble; comparative in Act 17:11, “more noble than those in Thessalonica.”
usage: “Their nobles put not their necks to the work of their Lord” — rank without labour, recorded for ever.
“The nobles of the people digged it” — the opposite picture, and the honourable one.
“These were more noble… and searched the scriptures daily” — nobility redefined.

pos: adj. (kingly, belonging to a king; rendering Hebrew melukah, Greek basileios)
etymology: From Latin regalis, from rex, king. In the New Testament the adjective is transferred to the church — a royal priesthood under a royal law.
biblical_def: Royal means belonging to a king, and the New Testament's startling move is to apply it to ordinary believers. Peter writes to scattered, persecuted congregations: “ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light” (1Pe 2:9). Every title once borne by Israel at Sinai is handed to the church, and priesthood is joined to royalty — not a priestly caste serving a laity, but a kingly priesthood of all who are in Christ. James supplies the law of that kingdom: “If ye fulfil the royal law according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, ye do well” (Jas 2:8) — royal because it is the King's own law, and because keeping it is the only sovereignty a subject is given. Isaiah adds the astonishing image of the church in God's own hand: “Thou shalt also be a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD, and a royal diadem in the hand of thy God” (Isa 62:3). The King wears His people.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines royal as kingly, pertaining to a king, becoming a king, and noble or illustrious — and notes the royal law of loving one's neighbour.
webster_full: ROYAL, a. Kingly; pertaining to a king; regal; as royal power or prerogative.
2. Becoming a king; magnificent; as royal state.
3. Noble; illustrious.
The royal law, the law of love, as prescribed by our King.
scriptures: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Jas 2:8
If ye fulfil the royal law according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, ye do well:
Isa 62:3
Thou shalt also be a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD, and a royal diadem in the hand of thy God.
For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called:
corruption_summary: The royal priesthood is read either as a licence for every believer to be his own church, or as a title reserved for clergy — where Peter gives it to the whole gathered congregation and gives it a purpose, to shew forth His praises.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome divides the priesthood, reserving the mediating office to an ordained caste and leaving the people to receive rather than to offer. Radical individualism divides it the other way, reading the priesthood of all believers as the private right of each Christian to need no church, no elders, and no accountability. Peter's grammar is against both: ye are a royal priesthood, a nation, a people — all plural, all corporate. The office belongs to the congregation together, which is why it shows itself in gathered worship, mutual confession, and the ordinances, not in solitary spirituality.

James guards the other flank. A royal priesthood is not a status to be enjoyed but a household under a royal law, and he introduces that law precisely while rebuking a congregation for seating the rich man well and the poor man badly. Royalty in the kingdom of God is proved at the door of the assembly, in how the least-dressed visitor is received. Peter says the purpose is to shew forth His praises; James says the test is whether you love your neighbour as yourself. Neither leaves room for a crown worn for its own sake.
roots_summary: Hebrew melukah (H4410), kingship, royalty; Greek basileios (G934), royal, kingly — the adjective Peter gives to a persecuted church.
roots_lines: Hebrew melukah (H4410) — kingship, royal estate; and meluwkah imagery behind the royal diadem of Isa 62:3.
Greek basileios (G934) — royal; “a royal priesthood” (1Pe 2:9), echoing Exo 19:6.
Greek basilikos (G937) — royal, kingly; the royal law of Jas 2:8.
usage: “Ye are… a royal priesthood” — Sinai's titles handed to a scattered church.
“If ye fulfil the royal law” — the King's own law, tested at the assembly door.
“A royal diadem in the hand of thy God” — the King wears His people.

pos: n. (a limb or organ of a body; a constituent part of a whole; rendering Greek melos)
etymology: From Latin membrum, a limb. Paul's ecclesiology is built on this word: the church is not an association of individuals but a body of members.
biblical_def: A member is a limb or organ — a part that has no life apart from the body it belongs to. Paul makes it the governing image of the church: “whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it” (1Co 12:26). Membership on this definition is not a club roll but an organic union in which another Christian's pain is felt in one's own body. The same word governs the doctrine of the body's holiness: “Know ye not that your bodies are the members of Christ? shall I then take the members of Christ, and make them the members of an harlot? God forbid” (1Co 6:15) — sexual sin is not merely rule-breaking but the dragging of Christ's own limbs into a union that dishonours Him. And James applies it to the smallest organ: “Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!” (Jas 3:5). A member is small, joined, and consequential — which is the whole doctrine of the local church in three words.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines member as a limb of an animal body, a part of a whole, and one of a community or society — the sense Paul gives the church.
webster_full: MEMBER, n. A limb of animal bodies; as a leg, an arm, an ear.
2. A part of a discourse, or of a period or sentence.
3. Any part of an integral.
4. A part of a community or society; as, every citizen is a member of the state.
5. In Scripture, a believer, as a part of the body of Christ.
scriptures: And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it.
Know ye not that your bodies are the members of Christ? shall I then take the members of Christ, and make them the members of an harlot? God forbid.
Jas 3:5
Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
corruption_summary: Church membership has been reduced to attendance, preference, or a name on a database, so that the very thing Paul used the word to exclude — a Christianity of detached individuals — is now the ordinary practice.
corruption_paragraphs: The consumer model of church treats the congregation as a service provider and the Christian as a customer who may sample, switch, or absent himself without injury to anyone. Paul's word forbids it. A hand does not attend the body on weeks when it finds the body edifying; it is joined, and its detachment is an amputation. This is why the New Testament assumes a definable congregation with known members and real elders — a body cannot suffer with a member it cannot identify, and church discipline is unintelligible without a roll it means something to be on.

1 Corinthians 6 shows the doctrine reaching into the body. Because the believer's limbs are Christ's members, what is done with them is done with His. That single premise settles more sexual ethics than any list of prohibitions, and it explains why Paul answers the Corinthian slogan about liberty not with a rule but with a fact of union. James then reminds us that the smallest member sets the largest fires, so that the tongue — gossip, slander, the whispered comparison — is precisely where the health of a body is decided.
roots_summary: Greek melos (G3196), a limb or member of the body — used of the believer's own limbs, of Christians in the church, and of the church in Christ.
roots_lines: Greek melos (G3196) — a limb, member; “whether one member suffer” (1Co 12:26).
The same word in Rom 6:13 — yield your members as instruments of righteousness unto God — makes the limbs the battleground of sanctification.
In Eph 5:30 believers are members of His body, of His flesh, and of His bones — the union grounded in marriage language.
usage: “Whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it” — membership defined by shared pain.
“Your bodies are the members of Christ” — the premise behind Christian sexual ethics.
“The tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things” — the smallest limb, the largest fire.

pos: adj. (appointed, formal, sacred, grave; rendering Hebrew mo'ed, atsarah)
etymology: From Latin solemnis, annual, stated, religiously observed. In the Authorized Version solemn usually means appointed — a day fixed by God, not a mood adopted by men.
biblical_def: In the Authorized Version solemn means appointed and set apart, not merely grave. The feasts are solemn because God fixed them: “in the day of your gladness, and in your solemn days, and in the beginnings of your months, ye shall blow with the trumpets” (Num 10:10) — and note that gladness and solemnity stand in the same sentence, with trumpets. The last day of Tabernacles is named outright: “on the eighth day shall be an holy convocation unto you… it is a solemn assembly; and ye shall do no servile work therein” (Lev 23:36). But an appointed day is no protection when the worshippers are false, and Isaiah records God's verdict on solemnity offered by bloody hands: “the new moons and sabbaths, the calling of assemblies, I cannot away with; it is iniquity, even the solemn meeting” (Isa 1:13). The word therefore holds together the two things the regulative principle exists to protect: that God appoints how He will be worshipped, and that appointed worship offered without repentance is itself an offence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines solemn as anniversary, observed once a year with religious ceremonies; religiously grave; marked with pomp and sanctity; and stated, established.
webster_full: SOLEMN, a. Anniversary; observed once a year with religious ceremonies.
2. Religiously grave; marked with pomp and sanctity; attended with religious rites.
3. Awful; inspiring awe.
4. Grave; serious; affectedly grave.
5. Sacred; enjoined by religion, or attended with a serious appeal to God.
scriptures: Also in the day of your gladness, and in your solemn days, and in the beginnings of your months, ye shall blow with the trumpets over your burnt offerings, and over the sacrifices of your peace offerings; that they may be to you for a memorial before your God: I am the LORD your God.

Seven days ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the LORD: on the eighth day shall be an holy convocation unto you; and ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the LORD: it is a solemn assembly; and ye shall do no servile work therein.
Isa 1:13
Bring no more vain oblations; incense is an abomination unto me; the new moons and sabbaths, the calling of assemblies, I cannot away with; it is iniquity, even the solemn meeting.
Psa 1:1
Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.
corruption_summary: Solemn has drifted from appointed by God to felt as serious by us, which hands the definition of worship back to the worshipper and quietly retires the regulative principle.
corruption_paragraphs: Once solemnity is a mood rather than an appointment, the question of corporate worship becomes what stirs the congregation rather than what God has commanded, and both wings go wrong at once. One side pursues atmosphere — lighting, swell, and staging engineered to produce the feeling of the sacred. The other pursues gravity for its own sake, mistaking severity for reverence. The Hebrew mo'ed cuts through both: a solemn day is a day God appointed, and its solemnity does not depend on how anyone feels about it.

Isaiah 1 then forbids the opposite complacency — that a divinely appointed form is sufficient in itself. Israel kept the calendar God gave and He said He could not away with it, because their hands were full of blood. The dictionary holds the regulative principle precisely because both halves are needed: God alone appoints the elements of worship, and He receives them only from those who wash and put away the evil of their doings. A church may have the right elements and still be told to stop.
roots_summary: Hebrew mo'ed (H4150), an appointed time or set feast, and atsarah (H6116), a solemn assembly — worship on God's calendar rather than man's mood.
roots_lines: Hebrew mo'ed (H4150) — appointed time, season, set feast; behind “your solemn days” (Num 10:10).
Hebrew atsarah (H6116) — a solemn assembly, closing convocation; the eighth-day assembly of Lev 23:36.
Hebrew miqra (H4744) — a holy convocation, a calling together; the summons that makes an assembly solemn.
usage: “In your solemn days… ye shall blow with the trumpets” — appointed, and glad.
“It is a solemn assembly” — the eighth day of the feast, work laid down.
“I cannot away with it; it is iniquity, even the solemn meeting” — right form, wrong hands.

pos: n. (a place of sitting; hence a place of authority or judgment; rendering Hebrew moshab, Greek kathedra, bēma, thronos)
etymology: Saxon set, from sittan, to sit. Because judges and rulers sat to give sentence, the seat became the standing figure for authority itself.
biblical_def: A seat in Scripture is rarely furniture; it is a position of authority, and the question is always whose. The psalter opens by charting a descent through three postures: the blessed man “walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful” (Psa 1:1) — walking, standing, sitting, each a further settling into the company. Our Lord recognises a legitimate seat and its abuse together: “The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses' seat” (Mat 23:2), an office to be respected even while the men in it are rebuked. There is a seat that belongs to the enemy: Christ commends the church at Pergamos for holding fast “even where Satan's seat is” (Rev 2:13) — faithfulness measured by its address. And there is the seat before which every one of them must finally stand: “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body… whether it be good or bad” (2Co 5:10). Every earthly seat is provisional. One is not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines seat as that on which one sits, a chair or bench; the place of sitting; a throne or tribunal; and hence the site of empire or of authority.
webster_full: SEAT, n. That on which one sits; a chair, bench, stool or any other thing on which a person sits.
2. The place of sitting; throne; chair of state; tribunal; post of authority.
3. Mansion; residence; dwelling; abode.
4. Site; situation.
5. That part of a thing on which another rests.
scriptures: Psa 1:1
Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.
Mat 23:2
Saying, The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses' seat:
Rev 2:13

I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is: and thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith, even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you, where Satan dwelleth.
For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad.
corruption_summary: The judgment seat of Christ has been quietly deleted from the believer's expectations, as though grace removed the appearing rather than removing the condemnation.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul writes “we must all appear” to Christians, and means it. Justification is complete and final — there is therefore now no condemnation — and yet the believer's works will be made manifest before the bēma, and he will receive according to what he has done in the body. Preaching that omits this in order to protect assurance ends by producing a Christianity in which nothing done in the body matters much. The Confession holds both without strain: the saints are perfectly and finally justified, and God will judge every man's work.

Psalm 1 and Revelation 2 give the two everyday applications. The psalm warns how gradually a man takes the wrong seat — he walks past it, then stands near it, then sits in it, and scorn has become his settled posture. Revelation warns that some believers are placed where the enemy's seat is and are expected to hold fast anyway; Christ names Antipas and does not promise Pergamos an easier address. Where a man sits reveals whom he serves, and one day it will be reported at a seat he did not choose.
roots_summary: Hebrew moshab (H4186), a seat, dwelling, assembly; Greek kathedra (G2515), a seat or chair, and bēma (G968), the raised tribunal of a magistrate.
roots_lines: Hebrew moshab (H4186) — a sitting, seat, dwelling place; the seat of the scornful (Psa 1:1).
Greek kathedra (G2515) — a seat or chair of office; Moses' seat (Mat 23:2), and the seats of the money-changers Christ overthrew.
Greek bēma (G968) — a raised platform or tribunal; the judgment seat of Christ (2Co 5:10) and Pilate's judgment seat (Joh 19:13).
usage: “Nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful” — the third and final step of the descent.
“The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses' seat” — the office honoured, the men rebuked.
“We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” — written to believers.

pos: n. (a young goat; rendering Hebrew gedi, Greek eriphos)
etymology: Of northern origin, a young goat. In Scripture the kid is the common man's festal meat, the standard small sacrifice, and the substitute that will not do.
biblical_def: A kid is a young goat — the ordinary household animal of celebration and of sacrifice. The Passover permitted it: “Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male of the first year: ye shall take it out from the sheep, or from the goats” (Exo 12:5). It was the meat of hospitality and of feasting, which is why the elder brother's complaint stings so precisely: “thou never gavest me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends” (Luk 15:29) — a man standing in his father's house, resenting a goat, blind to the fact that all the father had was already his. The law surrounded the kid with a strange tenderness: “Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk” (Exo 23:19), forbidding Israel to turn the source of the creature's life into the means of its cooking. And the kid appears at the hinge of the patriarchal deception, when Rebekah sends Jacob to “fetch me from thence two good kids of the goats; and I will make them savoury meat for thy father” (Gen 27:9) — the skins of a kid used to counterfeit a brother, and a family broken for twenty years by it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines kid as a young goat, and as the flesh of a young goat — both senses in constant use in the Authorized Version.
webster_full: KID, n. A young goat.
2. A faggot; a bundle of heath and furze.
KID, v.t. To bring forth a young goat.
KIDLING, n. A young kid.
scriptures: Exo 12:5
Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male of the first year: ye shall take it out from the sheep, or from the goats:

And he answering said to his father, Lo, these many years do I serve thee, neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment: and yet thou never gavest me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends:
The first of the firstfruits of thy land thou shalt bring into the house of the LORD thy God. Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk.
Gen 27:9
Go now to the flock, and fetch me from thence two good kids of the goats; and I will make them savoury meat for thy father, such as he loveth:
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What the kid recovers is the elder-brother sin — grievance nursed inside the father's house by a son who never asked.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The kid is ordinary realia: a young goat, eaten at feasts and offered at altars, and no modern movement has any interest in redefining it. What it does carry is a doctrine easy to miss, because the parable's sharpest line is about one.

The principle to recover is the elder brother's error, which is the besetting sin of long-standing church members rather than of prodigals. He had served many years, transgressed no commandment as he reckoned it, and burned over an ungiven goat — while living on an estate his father had already deeded to him. “Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine” is the answer, and it exposes the grievance as a failure to believe in the father's generosity, not a failure of the father's generosity. A man who has never asked for a kid has no standing to complain that he was never given one.
roots_summary: Hebrew gedi (H1423), a kid or young goat; Greek eriphos (G2056), a kid — festal meat, permitted Passover victim, and the elder brother's grievance.
roots_lines: Hebrew gedi (H1423) — a kid, young goat; the kids of Gen 27:9 and the prohibition of Exo 23:19.
Hebrew seh (H7716) — a member of the flock, lamb or kid; the Passover victim of Exo 12:5, drawn from sheep or goats.
Greek eriphos (G2056) — a kid or goat; the kid of Luk 15:29, and the goats set on the left hand in Mat 25:33.
usage: “Ye shall take it out from the sheep, or from the goats” — the Passover victim, lamb or kid.
“Thou never gavest me a kid” — grievance nursed inside the father's house.
“Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk” — mercy written into the kitchen.

pos: n. pl. (aromatic substances used in anointing, incense, and burial; rendering Hebrew besem, Greek arōma)
etymology: From Latin species, a kind or sort, hence goods of value. In Scripture spices are costly, fragrant, and always associated with consecration or with death.
biblical_def: Spices in Scripture are costly aromatics, and they mark the two solemn places: the sanctuary and the grave. God specified them for the holy anointing oil by name and weight: “Take thou also unto thee principal spices, of pure myrrh five hundred shekels, and of sweet cinnamon half so much… and of sweet calamus two hundred and fifty shekels” (Exo 30:23) — the recipe given, not invented, and reserved on pain of being cut off. The Song gathers them as the imagery of the beloved's garden: “Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices” (Son 4:14). And the women carried them to a tomb: “when the sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome, had bought sweet spices, that they might come and anoint him” (Mar 16:1) — love's last service, prepared for a body that was no longer there. The spices of the sanctuary consecrate; the spices of the tomb honour the dead; and on Easter morning the second use was made gloriously unnecessary.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines spice as a vegetable production, fragrant or aromatic to the smell and pungent to the taste, used in sauces and in medicine — and figuratively a small quantity.
webster_full: SPICE, n. A vegetable production, fragrant or aromatic to the smell, and pungent to the taste; used in sauces and in cookery.
2. A small quantity; something that enriches or alters the quality of a thing in a small degree.
SPICE, v.t. To season with spice, or with aromatic substances.
SPICERY, n. Spices in general; also, a repository of spices.
scriptures: Take thou also unto thee principal spices, of pure myrrh five hundred shekels, and of sweet cinnamon half so much, even two hundred and fifty shekels, and of sweet calamus two hundred and fifty shekels,
Son 4:14
Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices:
Mar 16:1
And when the sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome, had bought sweet spices, that they might come and anoint him.

Seven days ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the LORD: on the eighth day shall be an holy convocation unto you; and ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the LORD: it is a solemn assembly; and ye shall do no servile work therein.
corruption_summary: The holy anointing oil was a compounded formula God fenced from common use, and the modern appetite for anointing oils, sacred scents, and atmosphere-as-worship runs directly against the fence.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 30 does not merely list ingredients; it forbids replication. Whosoever compounded any like it, or put any of it upon a stranger, was to be cut off from his people. God gave the recipe and then closed it, because the fragrance signified a consecration He alone conferred. Modern religious commerce reopens it — anointing oils sold by the vial, sacred scents marketed for prayer rooms, atmosphere manufactured and then credited to the Spirit. The regulative principle applies to the nose as much as to the ear: what God has not commanded in worship is not ours to add.

The spices of Mark 16 point the better way. The women were doing the last kindness available to the dead, and it was a genuine kindness, bought at cost, carried at dawn. That they found no body to anoint is the gospel: the fragrance prepared for a corpse was left unused because the corpse was risen. Christian devotion is not less than theirs in love; it is simply relieved of the errand.
roots_summary: Hebrew besem (H1314), balsam, spice, sweet odour; Greek arōma (G759), fragrant spices for embalming — the sanctuary and the sepulchre.
roots_lines: Hebrew besem (H1314) — balsam, spice, sweet smell; the principal spices of the anointing oil (Exo 30:23).
Hebrew sammim (H5561) — sweet spices for the holy incense (Exo 30:34), likewise fenced from common use.
Greek arōma (G759) — spices, aromatics used in burial; the sweet spices of Mar 16:1.
usage: “Take thou also unto thee principal spices” — a recipe given by God and closed to imitation.
“With all the chief spices” — the garden imagery of the Song.
“Had bought sweet spices, that they might come and anoint him” — a kindness the resurrection made unnecessary.

pos: n. (a cord for measuring; hence a boundary, allotment, or standard; rendering Hebrew chebel, qav)
etymology: From Latin linea, a linen thread. The surveyor's cord gives Scripture its picture of an inheritance measured out and a standard laid against a wall.
biblical_def: A line is a measuring cord, and Scripture uses it for two things: what God allots and what God requires. Allotment first — the psalmist looks at the portion assigned him and says, “The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage” (Psa 16:6). The image is of a surveyor's cord stretched across a field to mark a man's inheritance; David is saying that God did the measuring and the measurement is good. Requirement second: “Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet: and the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies” (Isa 28:17) — the line is held against the wall, and every crooked course is exposed by a standard outside itself. Zechariah sees the same cord in an angel's hand for the measuring of Jerusalem (Zec 2:1), and the LORD Himself asks Job who stretched the line upon the foundations of the earth (Job 38:5). God measures what He gives and He measures what He judges — and in both cases the cord is His.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines line as a slender string, a thread extended to direct workmen; hence a boundary, a limit, and a rule or standard of conduct.
webster_full: LINE, n. In geometry, a quantity extended in length without breadth or thickness.
2. A slender string; a small cord or rope.
3. A thread or string extended to direct any operations; as the line of a mason.
4. Lineament; a mark in the face.
5. Limit; border; boundary; contour; outline.
scriptures: Psa 16:6
The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage.
Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet: and the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters shall overflow the hiding place.
Zec 2:1
I lifted up mine eyes again, and looked, and behold a man with a measuring line in his hand.
Job 38:5
Who hath laid the measures thereof, if thou knowest? or who hath stretched the line upon it?
corruption_summary: Contentment is now pursued as an attitude generated from within; Psalm 16 grounds it in a fact outside the self — the lines were laid by Someone else, and they fell where He meant them to.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern counsel on contentment is largely technique: gratitude practices, reframing, comparison management. Some of it is common grace and none of it reaches the root, because the root question is not how a man feels about his portion but who measured it. David does not talk himself into satisfaction; he observes where the cord fell and infers a Surveyor. Take away that Surveyor and the technique is a man persuading himself to like an accident, which is why it needs constant reapplication. <!-- voice-lock-ok: therapy: names the therapeutic frame to reject it -->

Isaiah 28 supplies the corrective on the other side, against a contentment that is really complacency. The same God who measures inheritances lays the line to judgment, and the builders of the refuge of lies discover that their walls were never plumb. A believer who is glad about his allotted lines and indifferent to the standard has taken half the doctrine. The cord in God's hand gives, and the cord in God's hand measures — and Job 38 reminds us it was stretched over the earth's foundations before any of us had an opinion.
roots_summary: Hebrew chebel (H2256), a cord, hence a measured portion or region, and qav (H6957), a measuring line — inheritance measured and righteousness measured.
roots_lines: Hebrew chebel (H2256) — a cord or rope, hence a measured allotment; “the lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places” (Psa 16:6).
Hebrew qav (H6957) — a measuring line, rule; “judgment also will I lay to the line” (Isa 28:17).
The measuring line reappears in the prophets as a sign of both rebuilding (Zec 2:1) and of destruction measured out (2Ki 21:13).
usage: “The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places” — contentment grounded in a Surveyor.
“Judgment also will I lay to the line” — a standard held against the wall.
“Who hath stretched the line upon it?” — the earth itself measured before we arrived.
